title: Identifying Single-Valued Functions via the Vertical Line Test
author: Muhammad Abdullah Athar
question: Which of the following algebraic equations defines y as a single-valued function of x according to the Vertical Line Test?

options.explanation: Incorrect. This represents a circle of radius 4; vertical lines x = c for -4 < c < 4 intersect the circle at two distinct points y = +-sqrt(16 - c^2).
options.misconception: Student equates geometric symmetry and smoothness with being a function, failing to recognize that a circle fails the Vertical Line Test because vertical lines intersect it at two distinct points.

options.explanation: Incorrect. Solving for y gives y = +-sqrt(x - 1), so for any x > 1 there are two corresponding y-values.
options.misconception: Student recognizes the quadratic relationship as a parabola but ignores the orientation, failing to see that a parabola opening horizontally along the x-axis fails the Vertical Line Test.

options.explanation: Correct! Solving for y yields y = 4 - x^2. For every real number x, there is exactly one unique real output y, so every vertical line intersects the parabola at most once.
Incorrect. For any x > -1/2, the equation yields two distinct outputs y = +(2x + 1) and y = -(2x + 1).
options.misconception: Student confuses the absolute value on y with an absolute value on x (y = |2x + 1|), overlooking that |y| produces two distinct outputs y = +-(2x + 1) for each positive input.

explanation: A relation defines y as a function of x if and only if each allowable input x produces a unique output y. In x^2 + y = 4, we can isolate y unambiguously: y = 4 - x^2. This describes a standard downward-opening parabola, passing the Vertical Line Test. The other equations all assign two values of y to a single input x.
